results.name: round_number_advantage
results.description: Among sets with no multiple-of-10 example, yes-rate on multiple-of-10 targets minus yes-rate on targets 1-4 away from a multiple of 10 (non-examples); observed > null means people favour round numbers beyond what the model's decade-boundary interval prior produces.
results.code:
# name: round_number_advantage
# description: Among sets with no multiple-of-10 example, yes-rate on multiple-of-10 targets minus yes-rate on targets 1-4 away from a multiple of 10 (non-examples); observed > null means people favour round numbers beyond what the model's decade-boundary interval prior produces.
def test_statistic(df):
    has10 = df["number_set"].map(lambda s: any(int(x) % 10 == 0 for x in s.split(",")))
    sub = df[~has10.to_numpy()]
    t = sub["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = sub["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    exs = sub["number_set"].map(lambda s: set(int(x) for x in s.split(","))).to_numpy()
    isex = np.array([tt in e for tt, e in zip(t, exs)])
    rnd = (t % 10 == 0)
    m = t % 10
    nb = (~rnd) & (np.minimum(m, 10 - m) <= 4) & ~isex
    if rnd.sum() == 0 or nb.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[rnd].mean() - r[nb].mean())

results.name: ap_congruent_minus_parity_matched
results.description: For sets of >=2 examples whose pairwise differences share a gcd g in 3..9 with nonzero offset (an arithmetic progression not captured by any multiple-of rule, e.g. 83,77 or 53,47,41), the yes-rate on non-example targets congruent to the examples mod g minus the yes-rate on same-parity non-congruent non-example targets within the same distance (<=3g of the nearest example); observed > null means people extrapolate step-progressions more than the model's rule space allows.
results.code:
# name: ap_congruent_minus_parity_matched
# description: For sets of >=2 examples whose pairwise differences share a gcd g in 3..9 with nonzero offset (an arithmetic progression not captured by any multiple-of rule, e.g. 83,77 or 53,47,41), the yes-rate on non-example targets congruent to the examples mod g minus the yes-rate on same-parity non-congruent non-example targets within the same distance (<=3g of the nearest example); observed > null means people extrapolate step-progressions more than the model's rule space allows.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = pd.Series(df["number_set"].unique())
    info = {}
    for s in sets:
        ex = [int(x) for x in s.split(",")]
        if len(ex) < 2:
            continue
        g = 0
        for x in ex[1:]:
            g = math.gcd(g, abs(x - ex[0]))
        if 3 <= g <= 9 and ex[0] % g != 0:
            info[s] = (g, ex[0] % g, ex[0] % 2 if len(set(e % 2 for e in ex)) == 1 else -1, ex)
    if not info:
        return 0.0
    sub = df[df["number_set"].isin(list(info.keys()))]
    t = sub["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    ns = sub["number_set"].to_numpy()
    g = np.array([info[s][0] for s in ns])
    off = np.array([info[s][1] for s in ns])
    par = np.array([info[s][2] for s in ns])
    exl = [info[s][3] for s in ns]
    dist = np.array([min(abs(tt - e) for e in ex) for tt, ex in zip(t, exl)])
    nonex = dist > 0
    near = dist <= 3 * g
    cong = (t % g) == off
    samepar = (par < 0) | ((t % 2) == par)
    r = sub["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    a = nonex & near & cong
    b = nonex & near & ~cong & samepar
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: between_set_yes_rate_sd
results.description: Standard deviation across sets (with >=20 trials) of the per-set yes-rate on non-example targets; observed > null means people's overall willingness to generalize varies more across example sets (some sets read as tight rules, others as broad) than the model predicts, observed < null means the model's set-to-set breadth differences are exaggerated.
results.code:
# name: between_set_yes_rate_sd
# description: Standard deviation across sets (with >=20 trials) of the per-set yes-rate on non-example targets; observed > null means people's overall willingness to generalize varies more across example sets (some sets read as tight rules, others as broad) than the model predicts, observed < null means the model's set-to-set breadth differences are exaggerated.
def test_statistic(df):
    exs = df["number_set"].map(lambda s: set(int(x) for x in s.split(","))).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    isex = np.array([tt in e for tt, e in zip(t, exs)])
    sub = df[~isex]
    g = sub.groupby("number_set")["rating"].agg(["mean", "size"])
    g = g[g["size"] >= 20]
    if len(g) < 2:
        return 0.0
    return float(g["mean"].std())

results.name: repdigit_target_advantage
results.description: Among sets containing no repdigit example (11,22,...,99), yes-rate on repdigit targets minus yes-rate on non-repdigit targets within +-3 of a repdigit; observed > null means people treat "same-digit" numbers as a salient concept the model lacks (observed < null: the model over-generalizes to them).
results.code:
# name: repdigit_target_advantage
# description: Among sets containing no repdigit example (11,22,...,99), yes-rate on repdigit targets minus yes-rate on non-repdigit targets within +-3 of a repdigit; observed > null means people treat "same-digit" numbers as a salient concept the model lacks (observed < null: the model over-generalizes to them).
def test_statistic(df):
    rep = {11, 22, 33, 44, 55, 66, 77, 88, 99}
    has_rep = df["number_set"].map(lambda s: any(int(x) in rep for x in s.split(",")))
    sub = df[~has_rep.to_numpy()]
    t = sub["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = sub["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    isrep = np.isin(t, list(rep))
    d = np.abs((t[:, None] - np.array(sorted(rep))[None, :])).min(axis=1)
    nb = (~isrep) & (d <= 3) & (t >= 10)
    if isrep.sum() == 0 or nb.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[isrep].mean() - r[nb].mean())

results.name: digit_reversal_target_advantage
results.description: Yes-rate on targets that are the digit-reversal of a two-digit non-palindromic example (e.g. 13 after 31) and not themselves examples, minus the yes-rate on other non-example targets in the same sets that share a digit with some example; observed > null means people use digit-permutation similarity the model lacks.
results.code:
# name: digit_reversal_target_advantage
# description: Yes-rate on targets that are the digit-reversal of a two-digit non-palindromic example (e.g. 13 after 31) and not themselves examples, minus the yes-rate on other non-example targets in the same sets that share a digit with some example; observed > null means people use digit-permutation similarity the model lacks.
def test_statistic(df):
    exl = df["number_set"].map(lambda s: [int(x) for x in s.split(",")]).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    rev = []
    shared = []
    isex = []
    has_rev_set = []
    for tt, ex in zip(t, exl):
        rs = set(int(str(e)[::-1]) for e in ex if 10 <= e <= 99 and e % 10 != 0 and e % 11 != 0)
        digs = set("".join(str(e) for e in ex))
        rev.append(tt in rs)
        shared.append(bool(set(str(tt)) & digs))
        isex.append(tt in ex)
        has_rev_set.append(len(rs) > 0)
    rev = np.array(rev); shared = np.array(shared); isex = np.array(isex); hs = np.array(has_rev_set)
    a = rev & ~isex
    b = hs & ~rev & ~isex & shared
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: small_target_yes_after_high_sets
results.description: Yes-rate on targets 1-10 for sets whose smallest example is >=30; observed > null means people generalize to small numbers far below the examples (via broad rules) more than the model predicts, observed < null means less.

results.name: inside_minus_outside_span_multi
results.description: For sets of >=3 examples, yes-rate on non-example targets strictly inside [min,max] of the examples minus yes-rate on targets outside that span; observed > null means people fill in the examples' span (interval-like generalization) more strongly relative to extrapolation than the model predicts.
results.code:
# name: inside_minus_outside_span_multi
# description: For sets of >=3 examples, yes-rate on non-example targets strictly inside [min,max] of the examples minus yes-rate on targets outside that span; observed > null means people fill in the examples' span (interval-like generalization) more strongly relative to extrapolation than the model predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    sp = df["number_set"].str.split(",")
    n = sp.str.len().to_numpy()
    mn = df["number_set"].map(lambda s: min(int(x) for x in s.split(","))).to_numpy()
    mx = df["number_set"].map(lambda s: max(int(x) for x in s.split(","))).to_numpy()
    exs = df["number_set"].map(lambda s: set(int(x) for x in s.split(","))).to_numpy()
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    isex = np.array([tt in e for tt, e in zip(t, exs)])
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    base = (n >= 3) & ~isex
    a = base & (t > mn) & (t < mx)
    b = base & ((t < mn) | (t > mx))
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: set_size_nonmember_slope
results.description: OLS slope of the yes response on number of examples (1-4) among non-example targets more than 10 away from every example; a more negative observed slope than null means people tighten generalization with more examples more strongly (stronger size principle) than the model, a less negative one means weaker.
results.code:
# name: set_size_nonmember_slope
# description: OLS slope of the yes response on number of examples (1-4) among non-example targets more than 10 away from every example; a more negative observed slope than null means people tighten generalization with more examples more strongly (stronger size principle) than the model, a less negative one means weaker.
def test_statistic(df):
    n = (df["number_set"].str.count(",") + 1).to_numpy().astype(float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    exl = df["number_set"].map(lambda s: [int(x) for x in s.split(",")]).to_numpy()
    dist = np.array([min(abs(tt - e) for e in ex) for tt, ex in zip(t, exl)])
    m = dist > 10
    x = n[m]
    y = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)[m]
    if len(x) < 3 or x.std() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.polyfit(x, y, 1)[0])
